course: Fortified Corn-Soy Porridge for Malnourished Children

lessons.title: Washing hands and utensils before preparing porridge
lessons.body:
Before you touch any food, you must wash your hands with soap and clean water. Use any soap availableâbar soap, liquid soap, or ash if soap is not available. Wet your hands, rub soap all over, including between fingers and under nails, for at least 20 seconds. Rinse with clean running water. If you don't have running water, pour water from a clean cup or bucket. Dry your hands with a clean cloth or let them air dry. Do this every time you start cooking, after using the toilet, after handling raw ingredients, and after touching animals.

Utensils must also be washed. Use a separate basin for washing. Scrub pots, spoons, bowls, and grinding stones with soap and clean water. Use a brush or sponge dedicated to cleaning. Pay attention to cracks and corners where food can hide. Rinse well with clean water to remove all soap. Then, if possible, sanitize by pouring boiling water over them or soaking in a mild bleach solution (1 teaspoon of bleach per 1 litre of water) for 2 minutes. Rinse again with clean water.

After washing, let utensils air dry on a clean rack or cloth. Do not dry with a dirty towel. Store them in a clean, covered place. If you have workers, show them this method step by step. Make it a rule: no one touches food or utensils with dirty hands. Keep a nail brush and soap near the washing area. In many African homes, a simple tippy-tap made from a jerrycan can provide running water for handwashing. This is cheap and effective.

Remember, germs are too small to see. Even if your hands look clean, they can carry bacteria that cause diarrhoea and other illnesses. Malnourished children are especially vulnerable. By washing hands and utensils properly, you protect the child and your whole family. Make it a habit, not a choice.

lessons.title: Keeping raw and cooked ingredients separate
lessons.body:
Raw ingredients like uncooked corn, soybeans, eggs, and meat can carry harmful germs. Cooked porridge is safe to eat, but if it touches raw ingredients or their juices, it becomes contaminated again. This is called cross-contamination. To prevent it, always keep raw and cooked foods separate.

Use different utensils for raw and cooked foods. For example, have one knife and cutting board for raw ingredients and another for cooked porridge. If you only have one, wash it thoroughly with soap and hot water after using it on raw food before using it on cooked food. Never put cooked porridge in a container that held raw ingredients without washing it first. Also, store raw ingredients in covered containers on the bottom shelf of your fridge or in a separate area from cooked food. If you don't have a fridge, keep raw ingredients in a cool, dry place away from where you store cooked porridge.

When preparing the porridge, grind or mill the corn and soybeans separately from any cooked food. If you use eggs or milk, keep them refrigerated until you are ready to cook. After cooking, serve the porridge immediately or store it in a clean, covered container. Do not let cooked porridge sit out for more than 2 hours. If you have leftovers, cool them quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours. Reheat thoroughly before serving.

In many African kitchens, space is limited. You can use colour-coded cutting boards or mark containers with tape to remind you. Teach your workers: raw on one side, cooked on the other. Always wash hands after touching raw ingredients. This simple separation can prevent serious illness.

lessons.title: Using clean water: boiling or filtering
lessons.body:
Water can look clear but still contain germs that cause diarrhoea, cholera, and typhoid. For making porridge for malnourished children, you must use clean water. The safest water is boiled water. Bring water to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute. If you are at high altitude, boil for 3 minutes. Let it cool covered before using. Boiling kills all germs. If you cannot boil, use a filter. Ceramic filters, biosand filters, or commercial filters can remove germs. Follow the manufacturer's instructions. If you have no filter, you can use chlorine bleach: add 2 drops of unscented bleach (like Clorox) per 1 litre of water, stir, and let it stand for 30 minutes. Or use purification tablets. Always store clean water in a clean, covered container. Use a ladle or cup to take water outânever dip your hands in.

For washing utensils and hands, you also need clean water. If water is scarce, use a tippy-tap for handwashing and reuse water for rinsing utensils only after it has been boiled or treated. Do not use untreated water to rinse utensils that will touch the porridge.

In rural areas, collect rainwater or use protected wells. If you use river or stream water, always treat it. Boiling is the cheapest and most reliable method. Make sure your workers know how to boil water and store it safely. Keep a covered pot of boiled water in the kitchen at all times. Change it daily. Never mix clean water with dirty water. Teach children to drink only clean water. By using clean water, you protect the child from infections that worsen malnutrition.

lessons.title: Cleaning your workspace and equipment daily
lessons.body:
A clean workspace is essential for safe food preparation. Every day, before and after making porridge, clean your kitchen or cooking area. Start by removing all food scraps and wiping surfaces with a clean cloth and soapy water. Use a disinfectant if available, or a bleach solution (1 tablespoon of bleach per 1 litre of water). Scrub tables, counters, and shelves. Don't forget corners and under equipment. Sweep and mop the floor. Empty rubbish bins and wash them. Keep animals out of the kitchen.

Equipment like pots, spoons, grinding mills, and storage containers must be cleaned after each use. Wash with hot soapy water, rinse, and sanitize. For grinding mills, disassemble if possible and brush out all flour residue. Dry equipment completely before storing. Store clean equipment in a clean, dry place, covered if possible. If you use a mortar and pestle, wash and dry it after every use. Never leave dirty utensils in the sink overnight.

Create a daily cleaning schedule. For example: Morning: sweep floor, wipe surfaces. After cooking: wash all utensils, clean stove, wipe surfaces. Evening: sweep again, take out rubbish. Assign tasks to workers if you have them. Check their work. Keep cleaning supplies like soap, bleach, brushes, and clean cloths in a dedicated area. Replace dirty cloths daily and wash them with hot water.

A clean workspace reduces flies, rodents, and germs. It also makes your porridge safer and more appealing. In many African communities, a simple routine like this can prevent disease. Make it a habit. Remember, a clean kitchen is a healthy kitchen.

lessons.title: Storing finished porridge to avoid spoilage
lessons.body:
After cooking, porridge can spoil quickly, especially in hot climates. To keep it safe, you must store it properly. First, cool the porridge quickly. Do not leave it in a large pot at room temperature for more than 2 hours. Divide it into smaller shallow containers to cool faster. Once cooled, cover tightly and store in a refrigerator if you have one. Set fridge to 4Â°C or below. If you don't have a fridge, use a cool, dark place like a clay pot or a evaporative cooler (zeer pot). You can also keep it in a clean, covered container and place it in a basin of cool water, changing the water often.

Porridge should be eaten within 24 hours if refrigerated. If kept without refrigeration, eat within 2 hours. Never leave porridge at room temperature for more than 2 hours. If you must store it longer, reheat it to boiling every 6 hours to kill germs, but this affects taste and nutrients. Better to make fresh porridge daily. If you see any mould, smell sour, or see bubbles, throw it away. Do not taste it to checkâit could make you sick.

When reheating, bring porridge to a rolling boil for at least 1 minute, stirring constantly. Serve immediately. Do not reheat more than once. For feeding malnourished children, always serve fresh porridge. If you have leftovers, cool and refrigerate within 2 hours. Label with date and time. Use within 24 hours. Teach your workers these rules. Use clean, food-grade containers with tight lids. Never store porridge in containers that held raw meat or chemicals. Keep storage area clean and free of pests. By storing properly, you prevent spoilage and keep the child safe.

lessons.title: Teaching hygiene rules to your workers
lessons.body:
If you have workers helping you make porridge, you must teach them hygiene rules. Start by explaining why hygiene matters: malnourished children can die from infections. Then, show them the correct methods. Demonstrate handwashing with soap for 20 seconds. Show them how to wash utensils with soap and hot water. Explain that they must wash hands after using the toilet, after handling raw ingredients, and after touching animals. Make it clear: no dirty hands touch the porridge.

Create simple rules and post them in the kitchen. Use pictures if workers cannot read. For example: a drawing of hands with soap, a drawing of a clean pot. Have daily reminders. Check their work. Praise good hygiene. Correct mistakes gently. Provide the tools they need: soap, clean water, brushes, clean cloths, and a handwashing station. If possible, use a tippy-tap. Assign one person to be the hygiene leader each day. That person checks hands and utensils before cooking starts.

Train workers on all aspects: keeping raw and cooked separate, using clean water, cleaning workspace daily, and storing porridge safely. Use a checklist. For example: Did you wash hands? Are utensils clean? Is water boiled? Is workspace clean? Is porridge stored properly? Go through the checklist together at the end of each day. Give feedback. If a worker is sick, especially with diarrhoea or vomiting, they must not handle food. They should rest and see a health worker.

Hold a short meeting once a week to review hygiene. Ask workers for ideas to improve. Reward good practices with small incentives. Remember, you are responsible for the safety of the porridge. By teaching your workers, you multiply your efforts. They will also teach others. In this way, you build a culture of hygiene that protects all the children you feed.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Safe Food Handling and Hygiene for Fortified Corn-Soy Porridge

In the production of fortified corn-soy porridge for malnourished children, food safety is not just a regulatory requirement â it is a business-critical control point. A single contamination event can sicken vulnerable children, trigger product recalls, destroy customer trust, and close your processing unit. In the African context, where cold chains are limited, water quality varies, and many processors operate semi-formally, hygiene discipline is the difference between a thriving enterprise and a liability. This reference module gives you practical, low-cost, verifiable hygiene controls you can implement today â whether you run a small household-based production unit or a growing registered food business.

1. Washing Hands and Utensils Before Preparing Porridge

Hands and utensils are the most common vehicles for transferring pathogens such as Salmonella, E. coli, and Staphylococcus aureus into porridge. Because fortified porridge is often consumed by children under five, even a low infectious dose can cause severe diarrhoea and worsen malnutrition. Establish a handwashing station at the entrance of your production area with running water (a tap with a bucket or a tippy-tap), soap, and a clean drying cloth or air dryer. Wash hands for at least 20 seconds, scrubbing palms, backs of hands, between fingers, and under nails. Utensils â mixing bowls, spoons, ladles, measuring cups, and sieves â must be washed with hot water and detergent, rinsed in clean water, and sanitised by immersion in boiling water for at least 30 seconds or by using food-grade sanitiser. Air-dry utensils on a clean rack; do not wipe with a shared cloth, which is a common source of recontamination in African food businesses.

2. Keeping Raw and Cooked Ingredients Separate

Cross-contamination between raw agricultural commodities (maize, soy, groundnuts) and finished or cooked porridge is a major risk. Raw grains and legumes can carry mould spores, aflatoxins, and bacteria. Store raw ingredients in sealed, labelled containers on lower shelves, and finished porridge or cooked ingredients on upper shelves or in a separate area. Use colour-coded utensils: for example, red for raw ingredients, green for cooked. Never use the same bowl or spoon for raw and cooked porridge without washing and sanitising in between. In many African processing units, the same mill or blender is used for raw and finished products â if this is unavoidable, establish a documented clean-down procedure between batches and verify it with a supervisor's signature.

3. Using Clean Water: Boiling or Filtering

Water is used for cooking, cleaning, and handwashing. If your water source is a borehole, well, river, or unprotected spring, assume it is contaminated. Bring water to a rolling boil for at least one minute (or three minutes at high altitude) before using it for porridge preparation or for rinsing utensils that will contact food. Alternatively, use a certified filter (ceramic, membrane, or biosand) followed by boiling if the source is highly turbid. Store treated water in a clean, covered container with a tap or ladle â never dip cups into stored water. Test your water source quarterly for total coliforms and E. coli using a local laboratory or a field test kit. Document results and corrective actions. This record is also useful for buyers and regulators who audit your food safety system.

4. Cleaning Your Workspace and Equipment Daily

Daily cleaning is a non-negotiable routine. At the end of every production day, sweep or vacuum floors, wash work surfaces with detergent and clean water, and sanitise with a food-safe sanitiser (e.g., diluted bleach at 100â200 ppm available chlorine, or 70% alcohol for small surfaces). Clean equipment such as mixers, mills, sealers, and drying trays. Remove all food debris from corners, under equipment, and in drains. Keep cleaning chemicals in a locked cabinet away from food. Maintain a cleaning schedule that specifies what is cleaned, how, how often, and by whom. In shared market spaces or community processing centres, assign a cleaning roster and post it visibly. A clean workspace also improves worker morale and reduces pest problems, which are costly to control.

5. Storing Finished Porridge to Avoid Spoilage

Fortified corn-soy porridge is a low-moisture product if properly dried, but if it is stored with residual moisture or exposed to humid air, mould and bacteria can grow. Cool the porridge completely before packaging. Use food-grade, airtight containers or sealed sachets. Store in a cool, dry, dark place, off the floor on pallets, away from walls, and away from chemicals or fuel. Label each batch with production date, batch number, and expiry date. For wet or semi-moist porridge, refrigerate below 5Â°C and use within 48 hours, or freeze for longer storage. In areas with unreliable electricity, consider solar drying to below 10% moisture and use oxygen absorbers or vacuum sealing. Conduct a daily check for pests, moisture, and off-odours; remove any compromised product immediately and record the loss.

6. Teaching Hygiene Rules to Your Workers

Your workers are your first line of defence. Train every new employee before they handle food, and refresh training quarterly. Cover handwashing, clean clothing and hair covering, no jewellery or nail polish, exclusion from work when sick (especially diarrhoea, vomiting, or open wounds), and proper use of gloves when handling ready-to-eat porridge. Use simple visual aids in local languages â posters, pictograms, and demonstrations. Keep a training log with names, dates, and topics. Empower a hygiene supervisor to conduct daily checks and correct unsafe behaviour immediately. Consider incentives for teams that maintain high hygiene scores; this turns compliance into a shared business goal. For small businesses, a one-page hygiene policy signed by each worker is a low-cost but powerful accountability tool.

â ï¸ RED SAFETY WARNING: Aflatoxin and Moisture Control

Never use maize, soy, or groundnuts that show visible mould, discolouration, or a musty smell. Aflatoxins produced by Aspergillus flavus and A. parasiticus are heat-stable and cannot be destroyed by cooking or boiling. They cause liver cancer, immune suppression, and stunted growth in children. In Africa, aflatoxin contamination is a leading cause of foodborne illness and export rejections. Test suspect batches with a rapid aflatoxin test kit (available from local agricultural extension offices) before processing. Store all raw ingredients below 13% moisture and in dry, ventilated conditions. If a batch tests above 10 ppb total aflatoxins for children's food, reject it entirely â do not blend it with clean stock. Document every rejection and inform your supplier in writing. This protects children's lives and your business licence.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • â Wash hands for 20 seconds with soap and running water before handling porridge, after toilet use, and after handling raw ingredients.
  • â Wash and sanitise all utensils and work surfaces before and after each production batch.
  • â Keep raw ingredients and cooked/finished porridge in separate containers, shelves, and utensils.
  • â Boil or filter all water used for cooking, rinsing, and handwashing; store treated water in covered containers.
  • â Clean floors, walls, equipment, and drains daily; keep cleaning chemicals locked away from food.
  • â Cool porridge completely before packaging; use airtight, food-grade packaging and label with batch number and date.
  • â Store finished product in a cool, dry, pest-free area off the floor; check daily for moisture, pests, and off-odours.
  • â Train every worker on hygiene rules before they handle food; keep a signed training log and refresh quarterly.

quiz.q: How long should you wash your hands with soap?
quiz.explanation: Washing hands for at least 20 seconds ensures proper removal of germs.

quiz.q: What should you use to dry your hands after washing?
options: C) A clean cloth or air dry
quiz.explanation: Using a clean cloth or air drying prevents recontamination of hands.

quiz.q: How often should you wash your hands during food preparation?
options: B) After using the toilet, handling raw food, and touching animals
D) Only if they look dirty
quiz.explanation: Hands must be washed at critical times to prevent contamination.

quiz.q: What is a cheap way to create running water for handwashing?
options: A) A tippy-tap made from a jerrycan
quiz.explanation: A tippy-tap is a low-cost, effective handwashing station.

quiz.q: How should you sanitize utensils if you don't have a dishwasher?
options: B) Soak in bleach solution (1 teaspoon per 1 litre) for 2 minutes
C) Wipe with a dry cloth
D) Leave them in the sun
quiz.explanation: A mild bleach solution kills germs on utensils.

quiz.q: Why must raw and cooked ingredients be kept separate?
quiz.explanation: Cross-contamination occurs when germs from raw food transfer to cooked food.

quiz.q: What should you do if you only have one cutting board?
options: A) Use it for both without washing
B) Wash it with soap and hot water after using for raw food
D) Wipe it with a cloth
quiz.explanation: Washing with soap and hot water removes germs before using for cooked food.

quiz.q: How long can cooked porridge sit at room temperature before it becomes unsafe?
quiz.explanation: After 2 hours, bacteria can multiply rapidly, making food unsafe.

quiz.q: Where should raw ingredients be stored in a fridge?
quiz.explanation: Storing raw meat and juices on the bottom shelf prevents drips onto cooked foods.

quiz.q: What is the safest way to make water safe to drink?
quiz.explanation: Boiling for at least 1 minute kills all harmful germs.

quiz.q: How much bleach should you add to 1 litre of water to purify it?
quiz.explanation: 2 drops of unscented bleach per litre is enough to disinfect water.

quiz.q: How long should you wait after adding bleach to water before drinking?
quiz.explanation: 30 minutes allows the bleach to kill germs.

quiz.q: How should you store clean water?
options: D) In a pot on the floor
quiz.explanation: A covered container prevents contamination.

quiz.q: What should you use to take water from a storage container?
quiz.explanation: Using a clean ladle or cup prevents introducing germs.

quiz.q: How often should you clean your workspace?
quiz.explanation: Daily cleaning prevents build-up of germs and pests.

quiz.q: What is a good disinfectant for surfaces?
options: A) Bleach solution (1 tablespoon per 1 litre)
quiz.explanation: A bleach solution effectively kills germs on surfaces.

quiz.q: What should you do with dirty utensils after cooking?
options: A) Leave them in the sink
B) Wash them immediately with soap and hot water
D) Stack them in a corner
quiz.explanation: Washing immediately prevents germs from multiplying.

quiz.q: How often should you replace dirty cleaning cloths?
quiz.explanation: Dirty cloths can spread germs; they should be washed or replaced daily.

quiz.q: Why should you keep animals out of the kitchen?
options: B) They carry germs and can contaminate food
quiz.explanation: Animals can spread harmful bacteria to food and surfaces.

quiz.q: How quickly should you cool cooked porridge?
quiz.explanation: Cooling within 2 hours prevents bacterial growth.

quiz.q: What is a good way to store porridge without a fridge?
options: A) In a clay pot or evaporative cooler
quiz.explanation: A clay pot or zeer pot keeps food cool and safe.

quiz.q: How long can you keep porridge in the fridge?
quiz.explanation: Refrigerated porridge should be eaten within 24 hours.

quiz.q: What should you do if porridge smells sour?
quiz.explanation: Sour smell indicates spoilage; eating it can cause illness.

quiz.q: How should you reheat stored porridge?
options: B) Bring to a rolling boil for 1 minute
quiz.explanation: Boiling for 1 minute kills any bacteria that may have grown.

quiz.q: What should you do before teaching workers hygiene rules?
options: D) Tell them to read a book
quiz.explanation: Understanding the importance motivates workers to follow rules.

quiz.q: How can you remind workers of hygiene rules if they cannot read?
quiz.explanation: Pictures are effective for non-literate workers.

quiz.q: What should a worker do if they have diarrhoea?
options: B) Not handle food and rest
quiz.explanation: Sick workers can spread germs; they must not handle food.

quiz.q: How often should you hold hygiene review meetings with workers?
quiz.explanation: Weekly meetings reinforce good practices and allow feedback.

quiz.q: What is a good way to check if workers are following hygiene rules?
quiz.explanation: A checklist ensures all steps are followed consistently.

quiz.q: Why is it important to teach hygiene to workers?
options: A) To protect the health of malnourished children
B) To make them work faster
D) To keep the kitchen tidy
quiz.explanation: Proper hygiene prevents infections that can be deadly for malnourished children.
